paras: The Pratt coal mines arrest shooting was the killing of an unnamed Black man by an officer at the Pratt coal mines in Jefferson County, Alabama, reported in a Montgomery dispatch of December 9, 1881. According to the dispatch, the man resisted arrest and took up a shotgun, and the officer shot him before he could fire. The item ran as a brief telegraphic crime notice in papers from Pennsylvania to Texas.

At the Pratt coal mines, an officer tried to arrest a man the dispatch called "a negro"; neither man is named, and no charge behind the arrest is given. In the fuller versions, the man refused "to go with him" and drew a shotgun, or in the New-York Tribune's wording "resisted and seized a shotgun." Before he could fire, the dispatch said, the officer "shot him fatally." The date of the shooting itself is not given.
No report of an inquest, arrest or other official inquiry into the shooting appears in the coverage, and no local Jefferson County account was found.

The story reached the white press as one short item from Montgomery, and each paper trimmed it differently. The Lancaster Daily Intelligencer printed it on December 9 under the headline "Killed While Resisting Arrest," mentioning only "resistance" and no weapon. On December 10 the New-York Tribune headed it "A Negro Shot and Killed" in a column of telegraphed crimes, while the Savannah Morning News and the Waco Daily Examiner folded it into roundups of brief and Alabama criminal news.

Every version gave only the officer's account and presented the resistance and the shotgun as fact. The Waco paper ran the item directly after a report from Chambers County that a crowd was going to the Lafayette jail to demand a Black prisoner accused of murdering a merchant.

The versions differ on the weapon: the Savannah and Waco papers said the man drew a shotgun, the Tribune that he seized one, and the Lancaster paper mentioned none. All four are condensations of the same dispatch, so none is better evidence than the others.

framing.detail: The Lancaster Daily Intelligencer headed it 'Killed While Resisting Arrest', putting the justification in the headline.
The New-York Tribune headed it 'A Negro Shot and Killed' among other telegraphed crimes.
The Savannah Morning News and Waco Daily Examiner ran it without a headline of its own in roundups of brief and Alabama criminal news.

conflicts.note: All are condensations of the same Montgomery dispatch; the variations are editorial and none is better evidence. All rest on the officer's side.
